c46_pro_thinking_004.label: Three Definitional Characteristics of a Real Option
c46_pro_thinking_004.description: For an asset or decision to contain a real option, it must have: (1) a clearly defined underlying asset whose value changes unpredictably, (2) contingent payoffs triggered by a specific event, and (3) a limited life.
coverage_criteria: List the three characteristics.
For a given business scenario, identify whether these characteristics are present.

c46_pro_thinking_005.description: An option only has significant economic value if there is exclusivity—the holder alone can exercise it. Without exclusivity (e.g., anyone can buy at market price), the option value is zero.

c46_pro_thinking_007.label: Replication and Arbitrage Principles in Option Pricing
c46_pro_thinking_007.description: Option pricing models rely on two principles: (1) replication—constructing a portfolio of the underlying asset and borrowing/lending that mimics the option's payoffs; (2) arbitrage—if two assets have identical payoffs, they must have the same price.
coverage_criteria: Describe what a replicating portfolio is.
Explain why arbitrage forces options and replicating portfolios to have equal prices.

anchors.locator: [11:26] Question 3: Can an Option Pricing Model Value the Real Option?

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video clearly states that all option pricing models are built on replication and arbitrage, defining each.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: These are two fundamental financial concepts that underpin the models; they can be checked with simple definitions and reasoning.

c46_pro_thinking_008.label: Trade-offs Between Black-Scholes and Binomial Models for Real Options
c46_pro_thinking_008.description: The Black-Scholes model assumes European exercise, constant variance, and no jumps, requiring only six inputs. The binomial model allows early exercise and changing variances but demands detailed price path data, often infeasible for real assets.
coverage_criteria: State the key restrictive assumptions of Black-Scholes.
Contrast the data requirements of the binomial model with its flexibility.
Articulate why practitioners might still prefer Black-Scholes despite its limitations.
